newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Solana briefs NATO allies on Russia deal.
newsitem.headline: Solana briefs NATO allies on Russia deal.

text.p: NATO Secretary General Javier Solana arrived back in Brussels on Wednesday after clinching a landmark NATO-Russia security deal and went straight into a meeting with NATO's 16 ambassadors to brief them on the details.
"I think honestly that the door is opened to a signing on May 27 in Paris," a smiling Solana told a large group of waiting reporters and cameramen.
NATO officials said the ambassadors would probably report back to national capitals after the briefing and the pact -- known as the NATO-Russia Founding Act -- would be formally approved on Thursday.
But first reactions from allied capitals were positive and around the world the deal was hailed as a major step towards securing a safe and peaceful Europe in the next century.

The White House applauded the news, saying the prospective agreement was something President Bill Clinton, a strong advocate of NATO enlargement, had fought for and worked hard on "for quite some time".
"We're obviously very encouraged," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.

Solana, who has negotiated the deal on behalf of the NATO allies with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, said he was sure the outstanding issues had now been resolved. He declined to give any details.

The pact inaugurates a new era in relations between the Cold War foes and is intended to answer Russia's concerns over the alliance's plans to take in new members from former communist Europe in July.
President Boris Yeltsin is set to sign the deal at a ceremony in Paris on May 27 with other alliance heads of government.

"It is a big victory for reason, it is a big victory for the world community and it is a big victory for Russia and all governments in the world interested in peace and cooperation," Primakov declared at a press conference in Moscow.

He clasped an arm around Solana at the news conference in the garden of a foreign ministry mansion in Moscow after the breakthrough which ended months of negotiations described by Solana as "very tough".
The agreement, intended to placate Russia before NATO invites new members in eastern Europe, was reached on the second day of the latest talks between the two men.
A joint statement said NATO and Russia had made "decisive progress" on key issues including military problems, which had been the main obstacles to agreement.
But it gave no details of the text, leaving lingering doubts over whether they had resolved their longstanding problems or simply agreed to gloss over them.
The two men had worked hard to agree the final details before the target date Yeltsin had set for signing the accord.
NATO officials were anxious to conclude a deal with Russia before a summit in July at which the Western defence alliance is expected to invite several former Soviet allies to join.
Russian leaders have spoken out strongly against NATO expansion, calling it a threat to its security.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to receive the first invitations to join NATO, although Romania and Slovenia also hope to be in the first wave.
